mcqs.question: Stripping away framework-specific details, what is the core axis the native-vs-cross-platform decision actually reduces to?
options: Engineering velocity from one shared codebase versus platform fidelity from no abstraction layer
Which framework has the larger open-source community
Whether the app targets iOS or Android as its primary platform
The programming language the team happens to already know
mcqs.explanation: Every other factor in this decision — team size, product category, release cadence — is a way of weighing which side of the velocity-vs-fidelity trade-off matters more for a specific product, which is the actual underlying axis. Community size and primary platform are secondary considerations, not the core trade-off itself.

mcqs.question: A startup is building an app whose core value proposition is a real-time AR camera filter experience. Why does this specifically favor native development?
options: AR and camera pipelines are impossible to access from any cross-platform framework
Cross-platform frameworks charge extra licensing fees for camera API access
The product's core value is exactly the platform-specific capability cross-platform abstraction layers cost the most to support and buy the least benefit from
Native apps are always cheaper to build regardless of feature set
mcqs.explanation: When the product's core value IS deep platform capability like real-time AR/camera processing, the abstraction layer a cross-platform framework adds costs the most exactly where the product needs the least abstraction. AR/camera access is possible via native modules in cross-platform frameworks, just with real overhead, and native isn't universally cheaper — it's a trade-off specific to this use case.

mcqs.question: A five-person startup needs to validate product-market fit with a content-driven catalog app, shipping to iOS and Android simultaneously every two weeks. What favors cross-platform here?
options: Cross-platform apps always outperform native apps in raw rendering speed
One shared codebase and release process directly serves the constraint of small headcount and simultaneous, frequent releases across both platforms
Native development is not possible for content-driven apps
Cross-platform frameworks are required by app stores for apps under a certain team size
mcqs.explanation: The specific constraints here — small team, simultaneous frequent releases, content-driven UI with little deep platform integration — are exactly what cross-platform's velocity advantage addresses well. There's no raw-speed superiority claim to make, no app-store team-size requirement, and native development is certainly possible for content apps, just costlier for this team's specific constraints.

mcqs.question: When comparing total cost of ownership between two native codebases and one cross-platform codebase, which factor do teams most often overlook?
options: Initial build cost, since it's always identical between the two approaches
Long-term framework risk — deprecation, breaking upgrades, or third-party library abandonment tied to a framework vendor's roadmap
The number of app store submissions required
Whether the app needs a backend API at all
mcqs.explanation: Cross-platform ties the app's future to a third party's maintenance trajectory in a way two native codebases don't, and that risk is easy to skip when comparing only today's feature set and initial build cost. Initial build cost is not identical between the approaches, and app store submission count and backend API needs aren't the distinguishing total-cost factors here.

mcqs.question: A team picks React Native because a popular conference talk praised it, without checking whether their product needs deep camera integration or whether their team has any JavaScript experience. What's the actual fix for this kind of mistake?
options: Switch to whichever framework has the most GitHub stars instead
Avoid all cross-platform frameworks permanently after one bad experience
Let each individual engineer choose their preferred framework for the parts of the app they own
Write down the product's actual constraints and the team's existing skill set first, then choose the framework that fits those constraints
mcqs.explanation: The fix is reversing the order: gather real constraints (day-one requirements, team skill set, realistic roadmap) before comparing frameworks, rather than picking a framework first and hoping it fits. Popularity metrics like star count don't capture a specific team's constraints, permanently avoiding an entire category overcorrects, and per-engineer framework choice fragments the codebase rather than fixing the underlying decision process.
